summary: Modest but sensible-looking recruitment befits the club’s new air of stability but a continuation of their spring slump could test David Moyes’s appetite for the fight
content: Guardian writers’ predicted position: 10th (NB: this is not necessarily Andy Hunter’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips) Last season’s position: 13th Prospects A season stripped of the fear of relegation, featuring more proactive, front-footed football and the return of some hope: had Everton been offered that package before their relocation to Hill Dickinson Stadium last summer it would have been accepted gratefully given the turmoil of the previous four years. For four fifths of last season it was accepted gratefully, but then came a collapse that transformed perceptions of David Moyes’s first full season back in charge. Talk of progress requires more supporting evidence this time around. Everton were three points off the fifth and final Champions League qualification spot on 21 March having dismantled Chelsea in their finest performance at the club’s new stadium. They did not win another game all season and slumped to 13th on the final day – the same position as the previous campaign under Sean Dyche and Moyes, with only one point more but an inferior goal difference. European football may well have been an ambitious target for a club adjusting to a new home and the loss of 10 players following the expiry of their contracts, loans included. But the opportunity presented itself to Moyes’s team and they blew it. Without the upheaval of last summer, with midfield resources improved and young players having had the benefit of a year’s experience of the Premier League, European qualification could be a more realistic proposition this season. Provided a few glaring holes in Moyes’s squad are finally filled. An upgrade on the limited centre-forward options of Beto and Thierno Barry is essential, although the latter has shown more promising signs in pre-season. Likewise a successor to Séamus Coleman – one of several big Evertonian losses behind the scenes recently. Everton’s quest for a new right-back is their very own Odyssey, while central defence was another area of concern last season. Genuine progress, the measure of which is not open to debate, rests on the final moves of the window. Off-field picture The consequences of Farhad Moshiri’s calamitous ownership are still being felt with Everton ordered to pay almost £40m in compensation to Burnley over the latter’s relegation in 2021-22. Everton are appealing against the can-of-worms verdict by a Premier League independent disciplinary commission, along with the biggest financial penalty ever imposed on a Premier League club, but claim their latest punishment has not affected this summer’s transfer plans. Many season ticket holders have been hit by above-inflation price increases – in some instances of almost 10% – and the club have extended a sponsorship deal with Stake, despite the UK government pledging to crack down on unlicensed gambling operators sponsoring British sports teams. Owner-fan relationship The Friedkin Group (TFG) has brought the financial stability that Everton desperately needed but it would be a stretch to suggest fans have connected with a low-key ownership group that rarely attend games. The man they appointed to run the club, chief executive, Angus Kinnear, annoyed supporters at the end of last season by claiming the hierarchy was “happily dissatisfied” with the first campaign at Hill Dickinson Stadium. The comment was portrayed as fresh evidence of Everton accepting mediocrity but in fairness to Kinnear, who was writing about TFG’s determination to banish the threats of financial instability, relegation and regulatory sanction, he did add: “The progress is clear but we have not achieved anything yet.” The manager David Moyes turns 64 in April and, while the Premier League’s oldest manager clearly retains the hunger and ambition to rebuild Everton on a stronger footing, it will be interesting to see whether he retains the appetite for a fight with his critics in the event of a poor start. Particularly as the Scotland job remains available and he would appear the ideal candidate to succeed Steve Clarke. Moyes was exceeding his brief until the dismal end to last season cost Everton a shot at Europe and placed his team selections under an unforgiving spotlight. Talk of a contract extension has since gone quiet. Star signing It has been a sensible window rather than a sexy one from Everton so far – see replacing Idrissa Gana Gueye with the £7m Christian Nørgaard – but they might have delivered in swapping Dwight McNeil for Brennan Johnson. No one would dispute that the Wales’ international’s move from Tottenham to Crystal Palace in January fell flat, least of all Palace who were willing to take a significant hit on their £35m, one-time record investment only seven months later. But if the 25-year-old recaptures the form he showed at Nottingham Forest, or when scoring 18 goals for Spurs in 2024-25, he could prove a steal who addresses several problems in the Everton frontline. Stat attack David Moyes loves to keep a settled side. Everton averaged the fewest changes to their starting XI of any team in the 2025-26 Premier League. With the squad looking largely the same as last season, this trend should continue. But what if injuries bite? Set for a breakthrough Tyler Dibling would have been a strong candidate for this category last summer following his arrival from Southampton for an initial £35m. It reflects a nonevent of a debut season on Merseyside that he can be nominated 12 months on. Everton invested a lot of time and money into their pursuit of the England Under-21 international, who remains the most expensive signing of Moyes’s second spell in charge, but the return was a huge disappointment. The attacking midfielder started only four league games and was not given a single minute after the 2-0 win over Burnley on 3 March. chineseTitle: 英超联赛 2026-27 预览第 9 名：埃弗顿
chineseSummary: 适度但看起来合理的招募符合俱乐部新的稳定氛围，但春季低迷的持续可能会考验大卫·莫耶斯的战斗胃口
chineseContent: 《卫报》撰稿人的预测排名：第 10 位（注意：这不一定是安迪·亨特的预测，而是我们撰稿人提示的平均值） 上赛季的排名：第 13 位 前景 一个摆脱了降级恐惧的赛季，以更加积极主动的足球风格和一些希望的回归为特色：如果埃弗顿在去年夏天搬迁到希尔迪金森体育场之前就获得了这一套餐，考虑到过去四年的动荡，它会感激地接受。上赛季五分之四的时间里，人们欣然接受了这一点，但随后的崩溃改变了人们对大卫·莫耶斯重新执教的第一个完整赛季的看法。这次谈论进展需要更多支持证据。 3 月 21 日，埃弗顿在俱乐部新球场的最佳表现中击败了切尔西，距离第五个也是最后一个欧冠资格席位还有 3 分的差距。他们整个赛季都没有再赢过一场比赛，并在最后一天跌至第13位——与上赛季在肖恩·戴奇和莫耶斯的带领下排名相同，只多了一分，但净胜球却较差。对于一家适应新家的俱乐部来说，欧洲足球很可能是一个雄心勃勃的目标，并且在合同（包括贷款）到期后失去了 10 名球员。但机会出现在莫耶斯的团队面前，但他们却搞砸了。如果没有去年夏天的剧变，随着中场资源的改善以及年轻球员在英超一年的经验中受益，本赛季的欧洲资格可能是一个更现实的提议。前提是莫耶斯队中的一些明显漏洞最终得到填补。对贝托和蒂埃诺·巴里有限的中锋选择进行升级是至关重要的，尽管后者在季前赛中表现出了更有希望的迹象。
